name: Automation landing page
summary: A single scrolling upsell page for partners who already sell SSL and want to move their existing book onto automation products. No catalogue, no validation explainers — one argument, one form.
audience: A partner's EXISTING certificate customers. They already understand what a certificate is. Do not explain DV vs OV to them.
job: Convert a manual-renewal customer into an automation subscription, using their own renewal workload as the argument.
constraints: This page sits on the partner's own site alongside their existing SSL page. It must NOT duplicate or compete with that page.

HARD RULE — where a partner has their own certificate-automation or lifecycle product, the outage-and-risk narrative is THEIR territory. Drop the risk framing and lead on effort saved instead. This was an explicit constraint on the UCERT deliverable and applies to any partner with a competing in-house product.
Never state a renewal count as fact. Compute it from the customer's own certificate count, or leave it as an input.

content.label: Hero
content.purpose: One sentence that makes an existing customer feel the recurring cost of their current process.

variants.tone: Effort saved — safe for partners with a competing product
variants.headline: Same certificates. None of the renewals.
variants.lede: You already buy your certificates from us. These are the same publicly trusted certificates, on plans where the key, the CSR, the validation and the installation happen without anyone opening a terminal.

variants.headline: Twelve renewals a year, per certificate, by 2029.
variants.lede: The 47-day cap is not a warning about the future — the first phase is already in effect. Every certificate you hold manually is about to need renewing roughly every month. These plans do it for you.

variants.tone: Risk — DO NOT USE where the partner sells a competing CLM product
variants.headline: The outage nobody scheduled.
variants.lede: An expired certificate does not degrade. It stops. As renewal frequency triples, the odds that one slips through a manual process stop being small.

content.widget_note: Date picker driving an animated track where each block is one certificate sized by the CA/B cap on its issue date. Counters: certificates in term, manual renewals, and zero with automation. Values computed from facts.validity_schedule.

content.label: The arithmetic
content.purpose: Turn an abstract policy change into the reader's own workload. This is the page's engine.

variants.headline: How many renewals are you signed up for?
variants.lede: Put in how many certificates you hold. The rest is the published schedule doing the maths.

inputs.label: Minutes per renewal, honestly
inputs.hint: Key and CSR, validation, install, reload, verify, diarise. Most teams underestimate this.

variants.honesty_note: The two-thirds factor reflects normal practice — teams renew before expiry, not on the day. State the assumption on the page. A calculator that hides its assumptions is a calculator nobody trusts.

content.label: How it works
content.purpose: Show that setup is small. The objection here is 'this will be a project', not 'I don't need it'.

variants.headline: Two ways in. Pick the one that matches your team.

routes.title: An agent on the server
steps: We place the order and send you a setup link
You install the agent on the server — one command
The agent generates the key and CSR, completes validation and installs the certificate
It repeats all of that every cycle, with nothing on your calendar
routes.note: Works on any server type. Not restricted to control panels.

routes.title: Your own ACME client
routes.for: Teams already running certbot, Caddy or cert-manager
steps: We place the order and send you EAB credentials — server URL, key ID, HMAC key
You register those credentials in the client you already run
Issue and renewal follow your existing pipeline

content.label: Plans
content.purpose: The product cards. Technical accuracy here is non-negotiable.

variants.headline: Six ways to stop renewing by hand.

grouping.subtitle: ACME only, many domains on one subscription

card_rules: Render the method tag from the product's methods array. +Automate reads 'Agent + ACME'; CaaS reads 'ACME only'.
Wildcard products must carry the DNS validation note.
Price is a slot. Render partner pricing or omit the row — never a placeholder figure.
No 'best seller' or volume badges. Positioning badges describing FIT are fine ('Best for teams', 'Linux admin favourite'); claims about SALES are checkable and must be true.

content.label: What it does not cover
content.purpose: Credibility. A page that claims automation solves everything gets discounted entirely by a technical reader.

rows.title: OV and EV stay manual
rows.body: These plans are DV. Anything that verifies your organisation still needs a person on both ends.

rows.title: Wildcards need DNS access
rows.body: DNS validation means writing a TXT record automatically — through a provider API or a delegated zone. Without that, wildcards stay manual.

rows.title: CaaS has no agent
rows.body: The Certificate-as-a-Service plans work only with an ACME client. If you cannot run one, take a +Automate plan instead.

rows.title: It does not find certificates you forgot
rows.body: Automation covers what you point it at. Certificates nobody inventoried are still the most common cause of an outage — audit first.

content.label: Lead form
content.purpose: Short. This reader is already a customer — do not ask for what the partner already knows.

variants.headline: Tell us what you are running and we will match a plan.
